scams.name: Fake Parking Ticket QR Code
scams.tldr: Scammers place realistic fake DC parking citations on out-of-state vehicles across Georgetown and the National Mall, with QR codes linking to fraudulent payment sites that charge $75–$150 and harvest credit card details for further unauthorized use.
scams.description:
Tourists with out-of-state plates parking in Georgetown, around the National Mall, and at Dupont Circle metered spots have found realistic-looking citations on their windshields. The fake tickets closely mimic official DC Department of Transportation citations — matching logos, city office names, and formatting — and are produced with handheld printers. Out-of-state visitors are targeted because they are unfamiliar with local parking rules and likelier to pay without questioning.

The ticket includes a QR code directing you to a payment website ending in .com rather than the .gov domain used by all official DC government sites. Victims who enter their card details lose $75–$150 in the immediate payment, then face additional unauthorized charges as the information is reused or sold. The DC DMV does not issue parking tickets; all legitimate citations come from the DC Department of Transportation or Metropolitan Police and can only be paid through official .gov sites.

The .gov domain is the one reliable tell. Never scan a QR code on a parking ticket — go directly to the official DC government website and search for any violation by your plate number. If you suspect a fake, photograph the ticket, report it to the DC DMV at (202) 737-4404, and dispute any charge immediately through your card issuer.
scams.avoidance: Only pay DC parking tickets through the official DC DMV website at dmv.dc.gov or by mail to the address listed on legitimate tickets. Check the issuing agency: legitimate DC tickets come from the DC Department of Transportation (DDOT) or Metropolitan Police, never from 'DC DMV.' Never scan a QR code on a parking ticket; instead, go directly to the official website and search for your violation by plate number. Take a photo of the ticket and compare it with official DC citation examples available on the DC government website. Report suspicious tickets to the DC DMV at (202) 737-4404 and file a complaint with the Better Business Bureau.
scams.location: Georgetown streets, National Mall parking areas, Dupont Circle metered spots, any street with out-of-state plates

scams.name: Metro Station Change Scam
scams.tldr: Scammers at Smithsonian and Gallery Place Metro stations ask tourists to break a $20 bill, then palm it and claim you only handed a $1, leaving victims $19 short with no recourse in a busy transit environment.
scams.description:
Inside busy Metro stations — Smithsonian, Gallery Place-Chinatown, and Union Station — a person approaches with a seemingly innocent request: they hold up two $10 bills and ask if you can exchange them for a $20 bill. The ask sounds trivial and helpful, and the surroundings feel safe enough to oblige.

When you hand over the $20, the scammer palms it and holds up a $1 bill, insisting that's all you gave them. A partner nearby creates a distraction — a bump, a dropped item, a sudden question — to cover the moment of the switch. Variants include asking to break a $50, then returning $5 bills folded to look like $20s. Losses of $19–$45 are too small to report, which is exactly the calculation the scammers rely on.

The defense is a single word. Never make change for a stranger in a Metro station — say a firm "no" without stopping and keep walking. If someone genuinely needs fare assistance, point them to the station manager booth. Keep large bills in a secure wallet and avoid displaying cash in crowded transit areas.
scams.avoidance: Never make change for strangers in Metro stations or on the street; politely say 'no' and keep walking. If someone needs Metro fare help, direct them to the station manager booth rather than giving cash. Keep large bills in a secure wallet and avoid displaying cash in crowded transit areas. Be especially alert at Smithsonian, Gallery Place, and Union Station Metro stops, which are prime hunting grounds. If you feel pressured, walk toward the station manager booth or a Metro Transit Police officer.
scams.location: Smithsonian Metro station, Gallery Place-Chinatown Metro, Union Station entrance, L'Enfant Plaza Metro concourse

scams.name: Unlicensed Pedicab Price Gouging
scams.tldr: Unlicensed pedicab operators on the National Mall quote no price before the ride, then demand $50–$120 at the destination, operating illegally on National Park Service property where the Tourmobile holds the exclusive transport contract.
scams.description:
Between the Capitol and Lincoln Memorial, pedicab operators approach tired visitors — especially families during cherry blossom season — offering a pleasant way to cover the two-mile stretch. The pitch sounds reasonable and the timing feels right when feet are sore and crowds are thick. Legitimate licensed operators like Nonpartisan Pedicab post their rates clearly at $84–$90 per hour before the ride; unlicensed operators quote nothing.

At the destination, the driver announces the fare: $50–$120 for a ten-minute trip. Some claim they charge $5–$8 per minute, a rate they never mentioned before boarding. The Tourmobile holds an exclusive transport contract on Mall property, making most pedicab pickups there illegal — but that fact offers no immediate help when you are being pressured for payment at the end of a ride.

Price before ride is the only safe sequence. Ask for the total fare in writing before boarding any pedicab, photograph the rate card and license number, and walk away from any driver who refuses to quote a price or says "we'll work it out after." Free alternatives include National Park Service ranger-led walks at all Mall memorials and the DC Circulator bus at $1.
scams.avoidance: Only use pedicab services that display clear per-hour pricing and are licensed by the National Park Service, such as Nonpartisan Pedicab. Always confirm the total fare, whether it is per trip or per hour, and get a verbal agreement before boarding. Take a photo of the rate card and the pedicab's license number before the ride begins. Walk the National Mall instead; the distance from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial is about 2 miles and manageable for most visitors. Use the free National Mall shuttle or DC Circulator bus ($1) as cheaper legitimate alternatives.
scams.location: National Mall between the Capitol and Lincoln Memorial, around the Washington Monument, Jefferson Memorial area, Tidal Basin during cherry blossom season

scams.name: Friendship Bracelet and CD Hustle
scams.tldr: Street vendors near the National Mall and Smithsonian museums tie bracelets on tourists' wrists or press music CDs into their hands without consent, then demand $10–$20 while accomplices use the distraction to pickpocket bags and pockets.
scams.description:
Near the Washington Monument, outside Smithsonian museum entrances, and on Georgetown's M Street, vendors approach visitors with a wide smile. They tie a colorful bracelet on your wrist before you can react — making friendly conversation to disguise the move — or press a music CD into your hands saying "it's free, just listen."

Once you have the item, they demand a $10–$20 "donation" and become hostile if you try to return it or leave. The more costly risk is the secondary one: a partner nearby uses the distraction to reach into your bag or back pocket. The confrontational dynamic pulls your attention forward while the theft happens at your periphery, making the bracelet itself a decoy.

Keep moving and keep your hands in control. Do not allow a stranger to place anything on your body — step back immediately if someone reaches for your wrist — and if a bracelet is tied on, remove it and set it down without argument or payment. Keep your bag zipped and across your front during any unexpected street interaction near the Mall.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands in your pockets or at your sides and firmly say 'No thank you' without breaking stride. Never allow a stranger to place anything on your body; physically step back if someone reaches for your wrist. If a bracelet is tied on, remove it and place it on the ground; you are not obligated to pay for unsolicited items. Keep your bag zipped and in front of you during any street interaction, especially near the National Mall. If someone becomes aggressive, walk toward the nearest Park Police officer or into a Smithsonian museum entrance.
scams.location: National Mall near the Washington Monument, outside Smithsonian museums, Georgetown M Street, Adams Morgan on weekend nights

scams.name: Three-Card Monte Gambling Hustle
scams.tldr: Street dealers near Union Station and Gallery Place run Three-Card Monte on cardboard boxes with planted shills who appear to win easily, drawing tourists into escalating bets of $50–$300 that are rigged through sleight of hand to always lose.
scams.description:
Near Union Station, along busy sidewalks off Pennsylvania Avenue, and around Gallery Place-Chinatown, a dealer shuffles three cards or shells on a cardboard box while a small crowd watches. Several "spectators" in the crowd appear to pick the winning card easily and encourage onlookers to try their luck.

Initial bets of $10–$20 are allowed to win, building confidence. When bets escalate to $50–$100, the dealer uses sleight of hand to ensure the winning card is never where it appears to be — a certainty, not bad luck. The Metropolitan Police Department is direct: "The only time you win in this game is when the suspect lets you, and the only reason they let you is to convince you that you can beat them." The team of four to six people — dealer, shills, and lookouts — can pack up and relocate in seconds when police approach.

There is no honest version of this game on a sidewalk. Walk past without stopping to watch — even standing as a spectator puts you within reach of pickpockets working the edges of the crowd. Report Three-Card Monte operations to Metropolitan Police at (202) 727-9099 or 911.
scams.avoidance: Never participate in street gambling games; the game is mathematically rigged through sleight of hand and you cannot win. Walk past without stopping to watch, as even spectators can be targeted by pickpockets working with the group. Understand that the people 'winning' are planted accomplices, not random lucky tourists. Report Three-Card Monte operations to the Metropolitan Police at (202) 727-9099 or 911. Remember that street gambling is illegal in DC and participants can be cited as well as victims.
scams.location: Near Union Station, Gallery Place-Chinatown sidewalks, busy intersections along Pennsylvania Avenue, downtown street corners

scams.name: Fake Tour Guide Solicitation
scams.tldr: Unlicensed self-appointed guides outside the White House, Capitol, and Lincoln Memorial charge $20–$50 per person for brief walks mixing basic facts with invented history, sometimes collecting cash upfront and disappearing after fifteen minutes.
scams.description:
Outside major landmarks — the White House on Pennsylvania Avenue, the Capitol steps, the Lincoln Memorial — individuals approach tourists presenting themselves as knowledgeable local guides. They quote $20–$50 per person for a personalized tour, target families with children by promising "kid-friendly" or "behind-the-scenes" access, and project enough confidence to appear legitimate.

Payment comes upfront in cash. The tour delivers fifteen to twenty minutes of basic facts available on any Wikipedia page, mixed with invented historical anecdotes. Some guides redirect the walk to souvenir shops where they earn commissions, spending more time there than at any memorial. Others disappear after a short circuit, citing a "schedule conflict." A common claim is that they hold "reserved spots" at attractions that are entirely free — the Capitol, all Smithsonian museums, and every National Mall monument charge no admission.

Every major DC attraction has a free official alternative. Book tours only through platforms with verifiable reviews like Viator or GetYourGuide, and take advantage of free National Park Service ranger-led walks at all Mall memorials. Never pay anyone who approaches you unsolicited outside a landmark, and remember that all Smithsonian museums and Mall monuments are free — no guide holds reserved spots.
scams.avoidance: Book tours only through established companies with verifiable websites, TripAdvisor profiles, and posted reviews. Take advantage of free National Park Service ranger-led walks and talks at all Mall memorials and monuments. Reserve free Capitol, White House, and Bureau of Engraving tours through official.gov websites well in advance. All Smithsonian museums are free; never pay anyone for 'skip the line' access to these institutions. If you want a paid tour, book through platforms like Viator or GetYourGuide where reviews and refund policies are transparent.
scams.location: Outside the White House on Pennsylvania Avenue, near the Capitol steps, around the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, Arlington Cemetery entrance

scams.name: Distraction Pickpocketing on the Metro
scams.tldr: Coordinated teams at Gallery Place-Chinatown and Smithsonian Metro stations use bumps, dropped items, and direction requests to distract tourists while partners lift wallets and phones, with losses ranging from a stolen phone to full credit card and identity exposure.
scams.description:
Gallery Place-Chinatown, Metro Center, and Smithsonian stations see constant tourist traffic — especially during cherry blossom season and Capitals or Wizards game nights — creating ideal conditions for distraction theft. Teams of two or three move through crowded platforms and escalators, watching for tourists consulting maps, holding phones out, or carrying unzipped bags.

One person bumps you, drops something near your feet, or asks a complicated question while standing unusually close. A partner uses the moment your attention shifts to lift your wallet from a back pocket, phone from an outer bag compartment, or passport from an unzipped pouch. The "sandwich" technique works escalators particularly well: one person stands close in front, another presses close from behind. Victims typically notice the loss only when they reach for their wallet at the next stop.

Closing the access points before you enter the station is the only reliable defense. Carry your wallet in a front pocket and keep your bag zipped and positioned across your front at all times on the Metro. Use a money belt or neck wallet for your passport and backup card during crowded station transfers. Report any theft immediately to Metro Transit Police at (202) 962-2121.
scams.avoidance: Carry your wallet in a front pocket and keep your bag zipped and positioned in front of your body at all times on the Metro. Use a money belt or neck wallet for your passport, large cash, and backup credit card when touring the city. Be especially vigilant on escalators at Smithsonian, Metro Center, and Gallery Place stations during peak tourist season. Keep your phone secured and avoid using it while walking through crowded station corridors. Report pickpocketing immediately to Metro Transit Police at (202) 962-2121 and cancel stolen cards right away.
scams.location: Gallery Place-Chinatown station, Metro Center transfer platform, crowded Orange/Blue/Silver line trains, Smithsonian station escalators
